item.title: Browzwear
item.description:
Browzwear helps clothing companies design digitally. In VStitcher, designers and pattern makers import 2D patterns, stitch them together virtually, and see the garment on an avatar with accurate fabric behavior. Changes to patterns or materials show immediately, and the 3D model can be checked for fit across sizes and body shapes.

The goal is to reduce physical samples, which are slow and costly. Teams can review a design with buyers using realistic renderings, adjust it, and send tech packs to factories, and the same files can feed marketing images. Browzwear also offers tools for fabric scanning and connections to product lifecycle management systems.

item.title: Heuritech
item.description:
Heuritech applies computer vision to fashion trends. Its models scan images from social platforms and recognize garments, colors, prints, and shapes, then measure how frequently each appears and how quickly that is changing. The output is a forecast of which items will grow or fade in a market.

Brands use the forecasts to decide what to design, produce, and stock, which can reduce unsold inventory. Reports are segmented by region, age group, and category, and the platform includes tools for tracking competitors and monitoring product performance against trends.

item.title: Stitch Fix
item.description:
Stitch Fix popularized personal styling by mail. A new client fills out a style profile, and a stylist assisted by algorithms selects pieces from many brands, ships them in a box, and the client keeps what they like and returns the rest. Feedback on each item improves later selections, and clients can also shop items directly through a browsing experience.

Data science has been central to the company’s identity. Algorithms analyze client preferences, item attributes, and inventory to predict what each customer will like, and stylists apply judgment and personal touches. Generative AI tools help create outfit suggestions and visual try-on features, and the company has also experimented with ways to let customers shop without a stylist.

item.title: CLO3D
item.description:
CLO3D, also known as CLO, replaces some physical sampling with digital prototypes. A designer imports or draws 2D patterns, stitches them together virtually, and sees the garment fall on an avatar with realistic fabric behavior. Changes to pattern shapes, colors, or materials show right away, and fit can be checked across sizes.

The software supports the work of a fashion team. It simulates fabric drape and movement, applies prints and trims, and produces renderings and animations for presentations. Files can be shared with colleagues and factories, and a related platform supports collaboration and asset libraries. Some automation assists with pattern adjustments.

item.title: Fashwell
item.description:
Fashwell works on a persistent problem in online retail: product data is often incomplete or inconsistent. Its AI looks at product photos and automatically identifies attributes such as category, color, pattern, shape, neckline, and material, creating detailed, standardized tags. Those tags help retailers organize catalogs, improve search, and power filters that match how customers describe items.

The same technology supports discovery features. Visual search lets shoppers find similar items from an image, recommendation systems suggest products that match a style, and outfit and style-matching tools help shoppers complete a look. Retailers use it to save the effort of manual tagging across thousands of items and to improve the consistency of information across channels.

item.title: The Yes
item.description:
The Yes used a swipe-based onboarding to learn a shopper’s taste in fashion and then curated a feed of products from many brands. Its algorithm tried to act like a personal stylist, adjusting to what a user liked and avoiding what they skipped.

Founded by a former Stitch Fix executive, the company was acquired by Pinterest, which folded the team and its taste-based personalization ideas into Pinterest’s shopping features. The standalone app and site were closed.

item.title: Vue.ai
item.description:
Vue.ai is built for retailers with large catalogs. Computer vision reads product images and assigns attributes such as color, pattern, neckline, fabric, and occasion, which saves teams from tagging thousands of items by hand. Those tags feed search, filters, and merchandising, so shoppers find items that match what they want.

The same data drives the customer-facing side. Recommendation engines suggest items based on browsing and purchase behavior, visual search lets shoppers upload a photo to find similar products, and styling tools suggest outfits that go together. Merchandisers can also see how products perform and adjust collections and layouts.

item.title: Outfit.fm
item.description:
Outfit.fm addresses the cost of fashion photography. A seller photographs a garment on a hanger or flat, uploads it, and the tool generates images of the item on virtual models in settings that suit the brand. Options include different body types, poses, and backgrounds.

Small brands and online sellers use it to fill catalogs and social feeds without booking models, studios, and photographers. Speed lets them test styles and update visuals frequently.
